To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) Humans learn a structured representation that facilitates continual task learning, and (b) augmenting deep neural networks with a generative model of the world reduces catastrophic forgetting under blocked learning.

(1) humans learn multiple tasks in succession by forming a factorized representation, (2) this factorized representation is a consequence of prior knowledge and training history, and (3) artificial agents can be designed to learn a factorized representation and thereby reduce catastrophic forgetting.

(1) humans learn better when training on one task at a time (blocked training) compared to interleaved training; (2) blocked training improves human learning by encouraging humans to form a factorized representation of the stimulus space that is optimal for the task; (3) deep neural networks trained with blocked training suffer catastrophic forgetting; and (4) adding a generative model that first learns a good representation of the stimulus improves continual task learning in deep neural networks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the cognitive processes that enable continual learning in the human mind and how these processes can be used to improve machine learning systems.
the development of computational models that can learn multiple task rules from experience and that are able to generalize across different tasks.
understanding and modeling the cognitive mechanisms underlying the human capacity for lifelong learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human brain is a continual learning system and that the human brain has the ability to form a representation that allows for continual learning.
the human brain can learn to perform a variety of tasks in succession over a lifetime, but current machine learning systems do not have this capability.
the results of this study demonstrate that humans can learn to perform a set of tasks sequentially and that they do so by forming factorized representations that are optimal for this task structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
humans can learn multiple tasks over their lifetime, but current deep networks cannot.
humans are able to learn multiple tasks in succession, whereas current machine learning models are not.
we found that humans can learn multiple tasks over their lifespan, and that they do so by first learning a good embedding of their environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human brain has evolved mechanisms for continual learning and these mechanisms can be exploited to build better artificial intelligence agents.
continual learning is possible for humans and that it is possible to build machines that can do the same.
the ability to perform multiple tasks is an emergent property that is built upon the ability to learn a structured world representation.
